passage:
“Why are you staring at them?” Thomas asked.

“I'm not staring.” Sarika pulled her lunch box closer. “I don't even like that game.”

“You've watched them for ten minutes.”

Across the playground the popular group burst out laughing, Kiara in the middle telling a story with big arms.

“They look so happy,” Sarika said quietly.

“You could go over.”

“They'll say something.” Sarika stood up anyway, brushed her skirt, walked a few steps, then laughed loudly at a joke she hadn't heard. Kiara glanced over and looked away.

Sarika came back and sat down. “Doesn't matter. I'm fine.”

Thomas offered half his orange. Sarika took it and did not eat it.

qa.q: How long had Sarika watched the group?
qa.a: Sarika had watched them for ten minutes.

qa.q: What does Sarika's “I'm fine” suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Sarika is hurt and longs to be part of the group but pretends not to care to protect pride.

qa.q: What could Sarika try next time instead of laughing at a joke not heard?
qa.a: Sarika could ask to join a game or stay with Thomas and find a game together, rather than trying hard to be noticed.

qa.q: What might Thomas be thinking as Sarika takes the orange and does not eat it?
qa.a: Thomas probably notices Sarika is upset and wants to help without pushing, so the orange is a way of staying close.

grounding: A child watches the popular group laughing, feels longing and hurt, tries to be noticed and then pretends not to care.

passage:
I'm Chandrika, and I was nine. At recess I sat on the low wall and watched Vinita's group play. They laughed so loud that my stomach hurt. Vinita had a shiny hair clip, and everyone wanted to stand next to her. I tried wearing a clip too. Nobody noticed. I told my friend Rani, “I don't care about them,” but I kept looking.

Once Vinita's group waved, and I waved back, and then I saw they were waving at the girl behind me. I laughed like it was funny. Rani was still beside me, holding my hand.

qa.q: What did Chandrika wear to try to be noticed?
qa.a: Chandrika tried wearing a clip.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika tell Rani, “I don't care about them”?
qa.a: Chandrika felt hurt and longing and pretended not to care so it would hurt less.

qa.q: What could Chandrika do after the wave that was not meant for Chandrika?
qa.a: Chandrika could turn to Rani, who was still there, and play with Rani instead of waiting to be noticed.

qa.q: What might Rani have thought watching Chandrika stare at the other group?
qa.a: Rani may have felt a bit overlooked and sad, wanting Chandrika's attention while Chandrika kept looking away.

grounding: A child watches the popular group laughing, feels longing and hurt, and pretends not to care.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, Wednesday.
At break, Vikas's group, the most popular boys, laugh loudly around the football. Tenzin stands near the pole, watching them. He laughs when they laugh, even though he can't hear the joke.
This week he has been telling very loud jokes in class, looking over at Vikas each time. When Vikas didn't laugh today, Tenzin's face fell, and he put his head on the desk.
When I asked him privately, he said, “I don't care about them anyway.” His voice cracked.
I have asked Vikas's group to include one new player each break, and I will give Tenzin the job of team scorer tomorrow so he's part of the game.

qa.q: Where does Tenzin stand at break?
qa.a: He stands near the pole, watching them.

qa.q: What does Tenzin's voice cracking suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: It suggests he does care, feeling hurt and longing to be included while pretending not to care.

qa.q: Why might the scorer job help Tenzin?
qa.a: It gives him a real role in the game without having to earn attention through loud jokes.

qa.q: How might Vikas see Tenzin's loud jokes?
qa.a: Vikas may not notice how much Tenzin wants to join, or may find the jokes a bit odd.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child watching the popular group with longing and hurt, trying too hard to be noticed and pretending not to care.

passage:
Tuesday
Kishore's group was doing that thing again at lunch, all laughing at some video on Kishore's phone, heads together. I sat two benches away with my tiffin.
I used to be in that group in Class 3. Before Kishore came. We used to make paper boats together.
Today I laughed really loudly at nothing, so they'd look. Nobody looked. Then I pretended I was reading my science book. I don't care. I don't even like that video stuff.
That's what I told Mummy too. But when I lay down, my chest hurt, like when you swallow something too big.
Maybe tomorrow I'll bring my new cricket ball.
Gautam

qa.q: What did Gautam and the group used to make together?
qa.a: They used to make paper boats together.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling while pretending to read?
qa.a: Gautam felt hurt and lonely, longing to be in the group again while pretending not to care.

qa.q: Is bringing the cricket ball a good idea, and why?
qa.a: It might help, since it offers a shared game, but Gautam could also find one friend from the group to play with first.

qa.q: How might Kishore's group see Gautam at the next bench?
qa.a: They probably don't notice much, busy with the video, unaware Gautam is hurting.

grounding: A child writes about watching the popular group with longing and hurt, trying to be noticed, then pretending not to care.

passage:
Every evening at the village well, the older girls played a clapping game and laughed so loud it echoed down the lane. Last year Devika had played with them. Now they were in the high school, with new jokes and new words, and she was still in the village school.
Devika sat on the steps of the temple opposite, pretending to watch the goats. She clapped the old rhythm softly on her knee.
Her friend Imran came by with his cycle. “Want to ride to the canal?”
“In a minute,” Devika said, eyes still on the girls.
One of them, Rekha didi, glanced over and waved. Devika's heart leapt. Then Rekha turned back to the game. Devika picked at a thread on her frock and didn't wave back.

qa.q: Where did the older girls play the clapping game?
qa.a: At the village well.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling as she clapped the old rhythm on her knee?
qa.a: She felt a mix of longing, nostalgia and hurt, missing the games she used to be part of.

qa.q: What could help Devika this evening?
qa.a: She could go with Imran to the canal and enjoy a friend who wants her company, instead of waiting on the steps.

qa.q: How might Imran feel when Devika says "In a minute"?
qa.a: He might feel a little ignored, since Devika's eyes are still on the older girls.

grounding: Shows a child watching the older popular group with longing and hurt, remembering being included and pretending not to care.

passage:
At recess in the Oslo school yard, Ulla's group sat on top of the climbing frame, sharing one pair of earbuds and laughing at something on a phone.
Rania stood by the fence with her lunchbox, pretending to read. She had practised a joke last night, a good one about the maths teacher's striped socks. She took three steps toward the frame, then stopped. Ulla glanced over, then turned back to the others.
Something in Rania's chest squeezed. She walked back to the fence and said, a little too loudly, to nobody, "Climbing frames are for babies anyway."
Then she read the same page of her book four times.

qa.q: What were Ulla's group sharing?
qa.a: One pair of earbuds.

qa.q: What was Rania feeling when she said "Climbing frames are for babies anyway"?
qa.a: Rania felt hurt and left out, and said it loudly to pretend she didn't care.

qa.q: What small step could help Rania at recess?
qa.a: A teacher or one of the group could invite her up with a simple "Want to listen?", or she could try the joke with one friendly person first.

qa.q: How might Ulla have seen Rania's three steps?
qa.a: Ulla may not have noticed much at all; to her it was a passing glance, not the big moment it was for Rania.

grounding: Shows a child watching the popular group with longing and hurt, trying to approach and then pretending not to care.
